measures.t: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO THE COUNTY OF ALLEGHENY HOME RULE CHARTER
measures.q: Shall Article III, Subsection 7(c) of Allegheny County's Home Rule Charter be repealed in order to remove restrictions on County Council members' ability to receive County funding for personal staff, district offices, and fringe benefits?
measures.s: Currently, County Council members receive a stipend in compensation for their service, but no funds for personal staff, local district offices, or fringe benefits such as health and life insurance, pensions, or personal motor vehicles. Other elected officers of the County do receive such benefits. The proposal asserts that this lack of financial support limits the field of individuals willing to run for Council. A yes vote would allow County Council members to eventually receive such benefits but does not immediately create a budget or funding allocation to support expenditures necessary to provide such benefits.
measures.sb: printed as the “Explanation of Ballot Question” in the Allegheny County Elections Division's list of ballot referenda; the list does not say who wrote it
measures.r: Decided at this referendum, as the Constitution of Pennsylvania requires for any amendment of a home rule charter; the share of votes it needs is set by the law under which the charter was adopted and is not stated here. (Pa. Const. art. IX, sec. 2)
measures.h: Put on the ballot by the governing body's ordinance or the electors' petition under the Home Rule Charter and Optional Plans Law. (53 Pa.C.S. sec. 2942)
measures.nt: Listed by the Allegheny County Elections Division in its ballot referenda for the November 2026 General Election (August 19, 2026), with the title and explanation it prints.

measures.t: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO THE MUNICIPALITY OF PENN HILLS HOME RULE CHARTER
measures.q: Shall the Penn Hills Home Rule Charter be amended to clarify the process for appointing an Acting or Interim Municipal Manager by distinguishing between a temporary absence of the Manager and a vacancy in the office of Manager, and to authorize Council to designate an Acting or Interim Manager in the event of a vacancy?
measures.s: Penn Hills’ charter currently allows the Municipal Manager to appoint an Acting Manager from within the municipality staff in the event of a temporary absence of the Manager of not more than 30 days. It does not address what should happen if the Manager fails to designate an acting surrogate or if a temporary absence goes beyond 30 days or becomes a vacancy. The proposed change allows the council to designate an Acting Manager from within the municipality staff if the Manager has not done so, or if the Manager’s absence from the office extends beyond 30 days or becomes a vacancy. Any Manager-designated Acting Manager’s 30-day appointment will terminate on occurrence of a vacancy but may be extended if reaffirmed by a vote of the Council. If the office of Manager is vacant because of resignation, removal, death, disability, or refusal to act, the Council may appoint a temporary Manager to serve until a permanent Manager is appointed. No Council member or elected officer may serve as Manager in any capacity. Appointment of a permanent Manager remains the responsibility of the Mayor.

measures.t: Malvern Borough: Home Rule Charter Referendum
measures.q: Shall the Home Rule Charter of the Borough of Malvern be amended to reduce the number of Members of Council from seven (7) to five (5) members, effective January 3, 2028, so that two (2) Members of Council are elected in 2027 and every four (4) years thereafter, and three (3) Members of Council are elected in 2029 and every four (4) years thereafter?
measures.s: The ballot question asks the voters of the Borough of Malvern whether the Home Rule Charter of the Borough of Malvern shall be amended to reduce the number of Council Members from the present seven (7) to five (5) members effective January 3, 2028. If this amendment is approved, the Home Rule Charter will also be amended to accomplish this change so that voters will elect only two (2) members, rather than four (4) members, in the 2027 election. The terms of the other three (3) present members will continue to January 2, 2030. The system of staggered election of members would continue. Three (3) members would be elected in 2029. The reduction in Council Members will not impact the existing term of any Council Member.
measures.sb: the “Plain Language” statement in Chester County Voter Services' official list of referendum questions; the list does not say who wrote it
measures.y: A vote of YES approves reducing the number of Malvern Borough Council Members from seven (7) to five (5) members and amending the nomination and election of Members of Council to accomplish this change.
measures.no: A vote of NO disapproves reducing the number of Malvern Borough Council Members from seven (7) to five (5) members and amending the nomination and election of Members of Council to accomplish this change.
measures.r: Decided at this referendum, as the Constitution of Pennsylvania requires for any amendment of a home rule charter; the share of votes it needs is set by the law under which the charter was adopted and is not stated here. (Pa. Const. art. IX, sec. 2)
measures.h: Put on the ballot by the borough council's ordinance or the electors' petition under the Home Rule Charter and Optional Plans Law. (53 Pa.C.S. sec. 2942)

measures.t: Tredyffrin Township: Home Rule Charter Referendum
measures.q: Shall the Tredyffrin Township Home Rule Charter be amended to: (1) delete “except for the first Board to serve under this Charter, the members of which will serve for staggered terms as provided in § 1201 of this Charter” from Art. II., § 202; (2) clarify that the office of Supervisor shall be forfeited if the person is convicted of a crime that is comparable to a misdemeanor of the second degree or higher under Pennsylvania law; (3) amend the rate of compensation for Supervisors from $1,500 to $3,000 per annum and remove the reference to the first four years that this Charter is in effect from Art. II., § 208(A); (4) clarify that notice of special meetings shall be prominently posted at the township office, and as otherwise approved by the Board; (5) clarify that a quorum of the Board may be established by in-person presence of Board members and by electronic means; (6) amend Art. II., § 210(C) to be consistent with the Pennsylvania Sunshine Act; (7) clarify that voting on ordinances and resolutions shall be by roll call vote of the Board and that all other votes may be by motion of the Board with each Board member’s vote recorded in the public meeting minutes; (8) provide that copies of the minutes of the meetings of the Board shall be available to the public at no cost; (9) amend that the meeting agenda shall be available at least twenty-four hours prior to the start of the meeting; (10) clarify that it is the duty of the Board to adopt an Administrative Code defining the organization and assignment of duties and responsibilities of township officers and employees; (11) clarify that it is the duty of the Board to initiate by motion, resolution, or ordinance inquiries and investigations in aid of its legislative functions; (12) abolish the elected position of Auditor and replace it with an appointed, independent auditor; (13) delete the following provisions in their entirety: Art. IV. Elected Tax Collector; Art. VI.(F) and (G); Art. VI. § C – 38(D); Art. VI. § C – 39; Art. XII., §§ C – 71and C – 72; Art. XII., §§ C - 73(B)-(C), C – 74, C – 75, and C – 76; (14) remove the Township residency requirement for the Township Manager; (15) require a proposed ordinance be advertised in one newspaper, unless otherwise required by law; (16) remove the requirement to provide notice to neighboring property owners of an amendment to the Zoning Ordinance applying only to a small portion of the township; (17) amend the effective date of an ordinance to immediately, or at any later date specified therein; (18) require copies of standard codes be available at the office of the township for public inspection with deletion of “and for purchase at a reasonable price fixed by the Board”; (19) remove the requirement that the general compilation be published “in loose leaf form”; (20) delete language requiring copies of “The General Laws of the Township of Tredyffrin” be furnished to township officers, placed in township libraries and the township office, and be made available for purchase; (21) remove language from Art. VII. § C – 44 requiring all changes in organization and procedures set forth in the Administrative Code be effected by amendment of the Administrative Code in the same manner as other ordinances; (22) amend Art. VII. § C – 45(C) to align with current practice; (23) require the Township Solicitor to be a member of the Bar of the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania in good standing; (24) amend Art. VII. § C – 46(B)(1) to require Board approval before the Township Solicitor acts as a legal advisor to other township officers, departments, boards, commissions, authorities and agencies and to clarify that a law firm is appointed not an individual attorney; (25) delete language addressing who is responsible for the duties of Finance Manager; (26) remove the requirement to advertise the preliminary budget, but require it be discussed and acted upon at a public meeting and be available for public inspection on the Township’s website or as otherwise required by law; (27) clarify the process for advertising and adopting the final budget and require that the final budget be advertised in one newspaper; (28) remove the requirement that the final budget be adopted by ordinance; (29) require that the budget be amended by resolution; (30) remove the capitalization policy which will now be in the Administrative Code; (31) require that all contracts of the Township involving sums in excess of an amount specified by the Board be by resolution; (32) require that the procedure for competitive bidding include advertisement in one newspaper; (33) clarify that competitive bidding is not required for, inter alia, contracts for labor, material, supplies or services aggregating less than the amount otherwise specified by the laws of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania; (34) update the categories in which discrimination is prohibited; (35) clarify that the statement of ownership of real property in the Township to be filed by Supervisors, the Township Manager, and their direct appointees does not include a principal residence; (36) specify which jurisdictions have comparable laws that disqualify a person from holding township office or employment; (37) clarify that any qualified citizen of the township may participate in the governing of the township by serving on boards, commissions, authorities, committees or other agencies of the township when “appointed”; (38) allow a transition period for any elected auditor in place prior to the adoption of the Charter amendment abolishing the elected auditor position; (39) otherwise make various changes to terminology; and (40) to otherwise amend numbering and naming of the provisions of the Charter and make other minor changes to wording.
measures.y: A vote of YES will approve the proposed amendments to the Home Rule Charter for the Township of Tredyffrin.
measures.no: A vote of NO will disapprove the proposed amendments to Home Rule Charter for the Township of Tredyffrin.
measures.r: Decided at this referendum, as the Constitution of Pennsylvania requires for any amendment of a home rule charter; the share of votes it needs is set by the law under which the charter was adopted and is not stated here. (Pa. Const. art. IX, sec. 2)
measures.h: Put on the ballot by the board of supervisors' ordinance or the electors' petition under the Home Rule Charter and Optional Plans Law. (53 Pa.C.S. sec. 2942)
measures.nt: Listed by Chester County Voter Services in its official list of referendum questions (updated September 14, 2026). The question bundles forty changes to the charter in one YES or NO vote. The county's plain language statement goes through the forty items one by one and is left to the linked list; its closing statement of what each vote does is shown.

measures.t: Conshohocken Borough Government Study Commission Question
measures.q: Shall a government study commission of seven members be elected to study the existing form of government of Conshohocken Borough, to consider the advisability of the adoption of a home rule charter, and if advisable, to draft and to recommend a home rule charter?
measures.s: Under Pennsylvania’s Home Rule Charter and Optional Plans law a question has been placed on the ballot asking voters to approve the formation of a government study commission consisting of seven members to study the existing form of government in Conshohocken Borough. If the commission is approved, the commission would determine if the adoption of a home rule charter is advisable. If the commission determines that the adoption is advisable they would recommend its adoption, draft a home rule charter, and the question of adopting the home rule charter would be placed on the ballot in a future election to be approved or rejected by electors of the borough. A majority yes vote on this question would allow for the formation of the study commission.
measures.sb: printed as the “Interpretive Statement” in Montgomery County Voter Services' notice of the question; the notice does not say who wrote it
measures.r: The study commission is formed unless a majority of those voting on the question vote against it; if a majority vote against, none of the candidates for the commission is elected. (53 Pa.C.S. sec. 2914)
measures.h: A question on electing a government study commission under the Home Rule Charter and Optional Plans Law; the same ballot elects its seven members. (53 Pa.C.S. sec. 2914)
measures.nt: Posted by Montgomery County Voter Services among its 2026 General Election papers. Voters in the borough also elect the seven members of the commission on the same ballot, whatever they vote on the question; that contest is not shown here.

measures.q: Do you favor the imposition of an increase in the earned income tax at the rate of twenty-five one hundredths of one percent (0.25%) to be used by the Township of Hatfield for the purposes of preserving undeveloped land and expanding opportunities for outdoor recreation; retiring indebtedness incurred in purchasing interests in real property and making additional acquisitions of real property for those purposes; and for expending funds for any purpose relating to the acquisition, planning for acquisition, preservation, improvement and maintenance of open space for an open space benefit?
measures.s:
Under the authority of the Open Space Lands Act, the Board of Commissioners of Hatfield Township is seeking voter approval to increase the current one half of one percent (0.50%) Earned Income Tax (EIT) already levied annually on residents of the Township by one quarter of one percent (0.25%).
…
If approved, the Township’s EIT would rise from 0.5% to 0.75%.
measures.sb: printed as the “Interpretive Statement” in Montgomery County Voter Services' notice of the question; the notice does not say who wrote it
measures.r: The open space tax may be levied only if a majority of those voting on the question vote in favor of it. (Open Space Lands Act, section 7.1(a.3))
measures.h: Put to the township's voters by an ordinance of the board of commissioners under the Open Space Lands Act. (Open Space Lands Act, section 7.1(a.3))
measures.nt: Posted by Montgomery County Voter Services among its 2026 General Election papers. This is Hatfield Township, not Hatfield Borough. The interpretive statement runs on about how the money may be used; two passages are shown (the rest is marked …) and the whole statement is in the linked notice.

measures.q: Shall the County of Lancaster establish a dedicated Library tax to provide for the maintenance of, and aid to, public Libraries in Lancaster County at the rate of .55 mills on the dollar on all taxable real estate within the County of Lancaster?
measures.s: Should a new countywide tax on all taxable properties, including but not limited to residential, business, and agricultural properties, be implemented strictly to support the public libraries of Lancaster County at a rate of $55 per $100,000 of assessed property value?
measures.sb: the “Plain English Statement” posted with the question by the Lancaster County Board of Elections; the page does not say who wrote it

measures.no: A NO vote on this question is AGAINST creating a new countywide tax strictly to support public libraries.
measures.r: The library tax is established if the majority of votes cast on the question approve it. (24 Pa.C.S. sec. 9315)
measures.h: Put to the county's voters under the Library Code, which lets a county or locality submit a library tax to its voters (the county commissioners may submit it, and must on a petition of 3% of the last election's voters). (24 Pa.C.S. sec. 9315 and 9302)

n.t: No statewide ballot question was found for the November 3, 2026 ballot in Pennsylvania, though no official page says so outright. The Department of State's upcoming elections page lists dates only, and a statewide question would come with the Attorney General's plain English statement, of which none has been published for 2026 (checked October 15, 2026). Pennsylvania has no citizen initiative.

Pennsylvania keeps no statewide list of local questions; each county board of elections prints its own. 13 local questions are shown, read from the county election offices of Philadelphia (two city charter changes), Allegheny (the county charter and three municipalities), Delaware (county land conservation debt), Chester (three townships and boroughs), Montgomery (two) and Lancaster (a county library tax). Bucks County's notice of the election lists offices only.

g.w: Local ballot questions in the other 60 counties

methods: lists

Who is running comes only from the Pennsylvania Department of State’s own lists of candidates for the November 3 general election and the May 19 primary, and the official primary results; each file is named below, with where it was read. The U.S. Senate and House races are on the Congress pages. County and local races are not loaded for Pennsylvania yet; they are loaded for 39 states so far, shown on the states page.
lists

What is read from the lists. The office and the district or place it belongs to, the candidate’s name, the party, the ballot order where the list gives one, the official primary vote counts where they are loaded, and the campaign website where a candidate listed one. Addresses, phone numbers and e-mail in the lists are never read, kept or shown.
lists
Parties. Offices elected on party lines show the party each candidate filed under, written out.
lists

Primaries. Where more people ran in a primary (May 19) than it could send on, everyone on that primary ballot is shown, with who went on to November, read from the general election list. Vote counts are the official results where they are loaded; where they are not, the race says so.
lists
Order. The lists read here give no ballot order. Candidates appear by surname. Never by money, polls or party.
holders

Who holds a seat today (the Legislature and the statewide offices the roster carries) comes from the Open States roster the record side of this site uses. A candidate matched to a sitting legislator by district and name, one fit only, links to their record page, and their birth date, terms and portrait come from that roster before anything else.
maps

The map and “use my location”. The lines on the map of “your ballot” come from the Pennsylvania Legislative Reapportionment Commission, the U.S. Census Bureau and the Pennsylvania Department of State (published on the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania's ArcGIS organization: precincts, the districts put together from whole precincts, and the larger districts’ own lines; each source’s own notice is shown with the map. The Legislature’s page draws the Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files. Your location is used on your own device to find your precinct and is never sent anywhere. The exact spot is not kept: what stays on the device until you tap “Forget” is your precinct with its districts and a rounded copy of the spot (about half a mile). A typed address goes from your device straight to the U.S. Census Bureau’s address finder, only when you press Look up; only the spot it finds comes back, used the same way, and this site never sees or keeps the address. Street pictures are off until you switch them on; then they come from OpenStreetMap’s servers, which see which map squares are asked for. Your county’s sample ballot is the authority on your ballot.
page
Nobody is scored or graded. The cards show the record; the judging is yours.
people

Who the candidates are. For statewide offices and the Legislature a card may show a photo, an age, the public offices a candidate has held, the government’s own page about an officeholder, the campaign’s website and the headings of its issues page. Official records come first; the rest was found on the open web by one reader and confirmed against the page that states it by a second, and a finding counts only when its source ties the person to this race. Each is labelled by its source and linked to it. Never collected, for anyone: home or mailing addresses, phone numbers, e-mail, family, marital status, religion, health, ethnicity, income, employers, schools or legal troubles. No social media profile, people-search site, data broker or voter file is ever a source, and nobody was contacted.
web

Found on the open web. A birth year or an office held is labelled by the kind of page that states it: “according to” a government’s own page or the campaign, “as reported by” Wikipedia or a named news organization. An age from a birth year alone reads “about”, and offices found this way are listed, never added up into years of service. A blank means nothing was found, not that there is nothing.
own

Campaign websites. A candidate’s website is the address they filed with the list, or the campaign’s own site found on the open web and checked against the race it names; the race’s page says which. An address that no longer leads to the campaign is left out.
own
In their own words. The topics a campaign’s issues page lists are shown as headings, with a link to the page; nothing is summarized. Photos from a campaign’s own site are credited to it and linked.
page

The record, not a label. For a nonpartisan office a race’s page shows only what is on the record: a party’s own published endorsement, an earlier run or office under a party label, and the candidate’s own words on their own campaign site, each linked to where it stands. This site never calls a person or a place by a party of its own choosing.
results

How a place has voted. For a nonpartisan office the race’s page shows how the place voted in past partisan elections: returns compiled precinct by precinct, close to but not the certified canvass (the sources say whose, and by how much they differ), added up here by county, city, town, borough or township and district on the lines in force at that election. It is not a prediction, it says nothing about any candidate or voter, and where very few people voted the split is left out.
polls

Polls of the statewide races are shown only from pollsters in the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative, who publish how each poll was done: the latest from up to five of them, each checked against the pollster’s own release, and our own average of the ten most recent, with the arithmetic shown. Polls by other pollsters are counted and named, not shown. A poll is a measure of opinion when it was taken, with a margin of error, not a forecast.
polls

Betting markets. Prices on Polymarket, a prediction market, are shown for the statewide races it lists, as information only: not a poll, not a forecast and not an official record. They are read from its public data, and prices move all day. Where Kalshi or PredictIt (two other markets) lists a race, the page says so and links to it, but shows none of its prices: their terms do not allow other sites to show them. A notice comes before any link to a market. The Civic Archive takes no money from any market and uses no referral links.
lists

The contests for Congress at the top of your ballot are the Congress pages’ own, from the state’s official candidate list: each name as printed, with its party label, in the ballot order the list gives (or by surname where it gives none), with its write-in and incumbent marks. Everything else about those candidates is on their race’s Congress page. Your U.S. House district is found from your precinct, where the map files place it, on your own device.
rules

Ballot questions. Each question’s official texts are shown word for word: the question as it will be printed and, where the record has them, the official summary, what a yes and a no vote do and the fiscal note, each labelled by who wrote it where the record says, and by its source. Where this site puts something in its own words (often the votes needed to pass and how the question got on the ballot), the question’s page says so beside it. Each side’s arguments in the official voter guide are linked, never reprinted.
page

Your ballot, printed or kept. “As it will look” draws your ballot as a printed sample ballot; it is a preview, not an official ballot, and your county’s own sample ballot is the authority. “Keep this ballot on my phone” saves the contests, the names, the questions’ words and the names of your districts and places in this device’s own storage, with the date, to open with no signal. No location, no address and no account: nothing is sent anywhere. “Forget my location and choices” removes it, and so does “Forget this ballot” on the kept page. Anyone holding your unlocked phone can see which districts a kept ballot is for.

changelog.title: Past results: Wisconsin, Minnesota's local races, and every precinct
items: Wisconsin's past results are here: Congress, the Legislature, district attorneys, statewide questions, and Milwaukee and Dane counties' own offices and questions, from the state Elections Commission's official files.

Minnesota now has every local contest of 2020, 2022 and 2024: judges, county offices, cities, townships, school boards, soil and water and hospital districts, and local questions, read from the Secretary of State's own result files (as kept by the Internet Archive after the count was certified) and checked precinct by precinct against the certified results.
Precinct by precinct: on the Past results page, open any county's or contest's precinct table to see each precinct's figures, for the 44 states that publish them. They load only when you open them.

changelog.title: Past results for every state, and the ballot in Spanish (a draft)
items: Past results now cover 49 states and the District of Columbia: the November general elections of 2020, 2022 and 2024, from President down to county offices, cities, townships, school boards, special districts and ballot questions wherever the state or county publishes official figures. Wisconsin's official files are not reachable yet, and the page says so.

Figures are shown by county and by city or town. Where a state's figures come from a compilation rather than its own official count, they are labelled secondary and no winner is marked from them. Where two official records disagree, both are shown and nothing is changed.
Each race page's "This seat before" now finds past elections in every loaded state.

On the draft site only: the ballot pages, menus, Help and the reading settings can be read in Spanish ("¿Leer en español?"). Each translated page says it was translated by Claude, an AI model, and not yet reviewed by a person. Names, office titles as printed and the words on your ballot stay in English; office titles show a Spanish translation beside the official English.
Ballot pages now say in one plain sentence what each office does, at the Beginner and Easy levels, with the official sources one tap away.

changelog.title: Past results: how places and seats voted in 2020, 2022 and 2024
items: New in Election Night: "Past results". Pick a state and a year (the November general elections of 2024, 2022 and 2020), then any contest on that ballot: names and parties as printed, votes and shares, the certified total and where it comes from, a county map, and the figures for each county, city or township.

North Dakota and Iowa are here in full, down to county offices, townships, soil and water districts and every ballot question. Illinois has Congress, the Legislature, judges and the statewide questions; Minnesota has President, Congress, the Legislature, Governor and the statewide offices. Their county and local races are next, and the page says which parts are still missing.

On The Ballot: race pages now have "This seat before", the same seat's past elections, with a note when the district's lines were different then. Ballot question pages have "Questions voters here decided before".
Every figure comes from the state's or county's official certified count and was checked against the official totals. Where two official records disagree, both are shown and nothing is changed.

changelog.title: The dashboard
items: New: a dashboard of the whole record, in three views. "Your place at a glance" shows any state or the whole country: what is on its ballot, who holds its seats, its ballot questions, and a link to its mail-voting facts. "The record, filtered" turns Congress's bills and floor votes into a sentence and charts you can narrow by chamber, topic and year. "Every state, side by side" puts all the states on one map, one measure at a time, with a two-state comparison.

Every figure is counted from the site's records when the page is built, and every chart says where its numbers come from and what they cannot tell you. Places can be compared; people are never ranked.
Beginner shows a few plain tiles; Medium adds the charts; Advanced opens the sources. Each view has its own address and a Share button.
The dashboard is linked from the home page, the menus, the On The Ballot door and Help.

changelog.title: Vote by mail, and questions answered
items: Every state's ballot page now has "Vote by mail or absentee": the last day to ask for a mail ballot and the last day to send it back for November 3, how to ask (the state's own link), how to send it back, what the envelope needs, how to track it, early voting in person, and what the state says for students at school elsewhere in the state or in another state, and for military and overseas voters. Every fact links to the state's own page or law and shows when it was checked. When a deadline has passed, the page says so and points to voting early or on Election Day.
"Your ballot" now says, under the election date, when to ask for a mail ballot.
The Congress ballot pages link each state to its mail-voting facts.

New: On The Ballot's questions page, with plain answers on voting by mail, students, military and overseas voters, moving, checking your registration, finding your polling place, when polls close, early voting, ID, tracking your ballot and a spoiled or lost ballot. Pick your state and each answer uses its own rules.
Every fact comes from the state's own election office or law, or from federal voting sites, and a second check re-read each source. The state election office always has the final word.

changelog.title: Share anything
items: Every part of the site now has a Share button: pages, races, ballot questions, counties, members, bills, votes, maps, the district lenses and Election Night. On a phone it opens your phone's own share sheet. On a computer it offers Copy link, e-mail, Facebook, LinkedIn, X, Bluesky, WhatsApp and Reddit (and text messages on a phone).
Nothing is sent until you pick a place. The place you pick then sees the link. No sharing buttons from those companies are loaded on these pages.
Every race, ballot question and county, down to the local contests, now has its own preview picture, so a shared link shows what it is about.
"Share my ballot" shares your precinct's ballot, after a note saying the link shows roughly where you vote. A shared link never carries your exact location.
The ready-made message sticks to the facts, for example: "U.S. Senate, Minnesota: who is on the November 3 ballot, from the official list."
